tagline: Two lanes among large oaks, plantation houses and an enduring parish church
intro: Ashley River Road narrows to two lanes through its scenic stretch, with large oaks and historic plantations beside the route. The Federal Highway Administration lists an 11-mile National Scenic Byway and allows 25 minutes for the drive or two days for places along it. Its profile emphasizes the historic district’s record of European and African settlement, commerce and industry.

Ashley River Road received a National Register listing in 1983. A 1998 state act designated a ten-mile section north of Church Creek Bridge as a scenic byway and prohibited off-premises outdoor advertising there. The landscape includes engineered rice fields: at Magnolia, enslaved Africans from rice-growing regions built the dams and dikes used to irrigate the crop. The river had served as a primary transportation route, carrying goods as well as people through the Lowcountry.

Traveling toward Charleston, begin with Middleton Place’s riverbank gardens. Magnolia comes next, where the Audubon Swamp Garden occupies a former reservoir for rice cultivation, followed by Drayton Hall’s surviving plantation house. Farther south, Old St. Andrew’s Parish Church stands near Church Creek, with a cross-shaped plan created by its eighteenth-century expansion. The church remains an active place of worship.

moments.title: Middleton Place
moments.text: Middleton Place’s Butterfly Lakes lie beneath terraces descending toward the Ashley River. The gardens were rebuilt over decades after John Julius Pringle Smith and his wife Heningham began restoring them in 1916. The main house did not survive: Union soldiers burned it in 1865, and the 1886 earthquake brought down its remaining walls. The present house was the south wing, repaired and converted into a residence after the war. The Middleton Place Foundation has researched the thousands of African Americans enslaved by the Middleton family. Bricks salvaged from the ruined main house were reused in the later stableyard complex.
moments.notice: The paired Butterfly Lakes resemble wings at the base of the garden terraces.

moments.title: Drayton Hall
moments.text: Drayton Hall’s double projecting portico faces the land approach from Ashley River Road, away from the river. Inside, a central entrance hall and divided staircase lead to a large salon, with chambers to either side. Its architecture follows Palladian models, including the symmetrical arrangement of the entrance hall, salon and surrounding rooms. The house belonged to an indigo and rice plantation whose grounds included thirteen cabins for enslaved people. Seven generations of Drayton heirs preserved the house, but its flanking service buildings were lost. An earthquake destroyed the laundry in 1886; a hurricane destroyed the kitchen in 1893.
moments.notice: The double portico faces the road approach, away from the Ashley River.

moments.title: Old St. Andrew's Parish Church
moments.text: Old St. Andrew’s began as a rectangular brick church in 1706; an expansion starting in 1723 turned it into a cross. The enlarged building tripled the floor space. Stucco concealed differences between the old and new brickwork and imitated a stone facade. A fire in the early 1760s left the walls standing, and the restored church reopened in 1764. Its altarpiece dates from that rebuilding. The fire restoration also gave the church its west-end balcony and stone-and-tile floor. The building remains in use for worship, retaining features of several periods of enlargement and repair.
